# 📘 Learning Guide: FizzBuzz

Read this before or alongside the README — the README assumes you know these concepts; this file teaches them.

---

## 0. How to use this guide

This is the first project in the repo, so this guide is deliberately the most patient one. It assumes **zero** JavaScript knowledge. If you already know what a `for` loop and a function are, skim section 2 and slow down at section 4.

Here is the route through this file:

| Section | What it does | Read it when |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What FizzBuzz is and why it's project 01 | First |
| 2 | Every concept the code uses, taught from scratch | Before you read any code |
| 3 | Line-by-line walkthrough of `original.js` | With the file open beside you |
| 4 | What's wrong with the original, in plain language | After you've formed your own opinion |
| 5 | Graded hints so you can fix it yourself | **Before** you look at `refactored/` |
| 6 | Line-by-line walkthrough of the refactor | After you've attempted it |
| 7 | Designs we considered and rejected | When you're wondering "why not do it *this* way?" |
| 8 | How the test file works and how to read a failure | Before you write your own tests |
| 9 | Where this pattern shows up in real software | When you want to know why this matters |
| 10 | Mistakes beginners actually make here, with real error text | When something breaks |
| 11 | Self-check questions with answers | To find out if it stuck |
| 12 | Glossary | Any time a word is unfamiliar |
| 13 | Experiments to run offline | Last — this is where the learning sticks |

**A warning about section 5.** The single most common way to waste this repo is to read the refactored code before trying to write it. Reading a solution feels like learning and isn't. You need the experience of being stuck, because that's what makes the solution memorable. Give yourself fifteen real minutes with section 5 before you scroll past it.

### What you need installed

Nothing but Node. Check you have it:

```
node --version
```

You want `v20` or higher (the repo is tested on `v22`). If that command errors, install Node from nodejs.org — it's the only dependency the JavaScript track has.

---

## 1. What are we building?

FizzBuzz is a classic counting game turned into a program. The program counts from 1 to 100 and prints one line per number, but with three special rules:

- If the number divides evenly by 3, print `Fizz` instead of the number.
- If it divides evenly by 5, print `Buzz` instead.
- If it divides evenly by *both* 3 and 5, print `FizzBuzz`.

So when you run it, the output starts like this:

```
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz
```

That's the whole program. It sounds trivial, but it's the perfect place to learn the single most important habit in this repo: keeping "figuring out the answer" separate from "printing the answer."

### Why FizzBuzz, of all things?

FizzBuzz became famous in 2007 when a programmer named Imran Ghory wrote about using it to screen job candidates, and Jeff Atwood amplified it. The claim that shocked people was that a large fraction of applicants for programming jobs could not write it. That reputation is why you'll sometimes see FizzBuzz treated as a joke or an insult.

That is **not** why it's here. We're not using it to test whether you can code. We're using it because it is the smallest program in existence that still has a real design decision in it. Look at how little there is: one loop, three rules, one output. And yet, as you'll see in section 4, there are at least six different ways to structure it, and they differ enormously in how easy they are to change. A program small enough to hold entirely in your head, that still rewards good design, is a rare and valuable teaching object.

Every later project in this repo is the same lesson wearing a bigger costume. Snake, the JSON parser, the React store — all of them are "separate deciding from doing." FizzBuzz is where you meet the idea while it's still small enough to see all of at once.

### The thing to watch for

As you read, keep one question in your head, and let it nag you:

> **How would I test this?**

That question is the whole course. It is not a question about testing. It is a question about *design*, wearing a testing disguise. Code that's hard to test is hard to test because it's tangled, and tangled code is hard to change. The test is just the messenger.

---

## 2. Concepts you need first

This section is a reference. You don't need to memorise it — read it once, then come back when a piece of code confuses you.

### Values and types

Everything in a JavaScript program is a **value**. Values come in kinds, called **types**. You only need four right now:

```js
42          // a number
"Fizz"      // a string (text) — quotes make it a string
true        // a boolean (true or false)
[1, 2, 3]   // an array (an ordered list of values)
```

Note carefully: `42` and `"42"` are **different values of different types**. One is a number you can do arithmetic with; the other is two text characters. Confusing them is the source of a genuinely enormous share of beginner bugs, and it's exactly what `===` (below) protects you from.

You can ask JavaScript what type something is:

```js
console.log(typeof 42);      // "number"
console.log(typeof "Fizz");  // "string"
console.log(typeof true);    // "boolean"
```

### Variables: `var`, `let`, and `const`

A **variable** is a named box that holds a value. JavaScript has three keywords to create one:

```js
var oldStyle = 1;   // the old way — avoid it (you'll see why below)
let counter = 2;    // a box whose contents you plan to change
const name = "Sam"; // a box you promise not to reassign
```

`let` and `const` are "block-scoped": they only exist inside the nearest pair of `{ }` curly braces. `var` ignores those braces and leaks out — a common source of confusing bugs.

Here's the leak, concretely:

```js
{
  var leaky = "I escaped";
  let contained = "I did not";
}
console.log(leaky);     // "I escaped"  — still here!
console.log(contained); // ReferenceError: contained is not defined
```

That `ReferenceError` is the **good** outcome. It's JavaScript telling you "you're using something outside the region where it makes sense." `var` stays silent and lets you make the mistake.

**Which should you use?** The rule practising programmers actually follow:

1. Use `const` by default.
2. Use `let` only when you genuinely need to reassign.
3. Never use `var`.

`const` first sounds restrictive but it's the opposite — it's information. When you see `const`, you know that name means the same thing for the rest of the block, so you can stop tracking it. Every `let` is a small tax on the reader's attention.

**A subtlety about `const` and arrays.** `const` means you can't *reassign the box*. It doesn't mean the contents are frozen:

```js
const parts = [];
parts.push('Fizz');  // ✅ fine — we changed what's IN the array
console.log(parts);  // ['Fizz']

parts = ['Buzz'];    // ❌ TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
```

This matters immediately, because the refactored `fizzbuzz.js` says `const parts = []` and then pushes into it. That is correct and idiomatic — not a loophole.

### The `%` operator (remainder / modulo)

`a % b` gives you the **remainder** after dividing `a` by `b`:

```js
console.log(10 % 3); // 1  (10 ÷ 3 = 3, remainder 1)
console.log(9 % 3);  // 0  (divides evenly — no remainder)
console.log(7 % 5);  // 2
console.log(15 % 5); // 0
console.log(15 % 3); // 0  (15 is a multiple of both — this is why 15 is FizzBuzz)
```

The key trick: `n % 3 === 0` means "n is a multiple of 3." That's how FizzBuzz detects its special numbers.

It helps to picture it as repeated subtraction. `17 % 5`: subtract 5 to get 12, subtract 5 to get 7, subtract 5 to get 2 — can't subtract again, so the answer is 2.

**A gotcha worth knowing now.** With negative numbers, JavaScript's `%` keeps the sign of the left-hand side:

```js
console.log(-9 % 3);  // -0   (which === 0, so the check still works)
console.log(-10 % 3); // -1   (NOT 2, which is what a mathematician might expect)
```

FizzBuzz counts upward from 1 so this never bites here — but it's the kind of thing that bites later, and PRACTICE.md exercise 1 makes you think about it.

### Comparison operators

```js
1 === 1     // true
1 !== 2     // true   (!== is "not equal")
3 < 5       // true
5 <= 5      // true
```

These produce booleans, which is what `if` needs.

### `==` vs `===` (loose vs strict equality)

`==` converts types before comparing. `===` doesn't.

```js
"3" == 3    // true  😱  — the string got converted to a number
"3" === 3   // false ✅  — different types, so not equal
0 == false  // true  😱
0 === false // false ✅
null == undefined  // true 😱
null === undefined // false ✅
```

**Always use `===` and `!==`.** The rule has no useful exceptions for a beginner. `==` has a genuinely baroque conversion table that even experienced developers misremember, and every "convenience" it offers is a place a type bug can hide.

Why does the original file's `==` not cause a bug today? Because `i` is always a number and `0` is always a number, so there's nothing to convert. It's not wrong *yet*. It's a habit that will be wrong the first time input arrives from a file, a form, or a network request — because all three of those hand you **strings**.

### `if` / `else if` / `else`

These let a program choose between paths:

```js
if (temperature > 30) {
  console.log("hot");
} else if (temperature > 20) {
  console.log("warm");
} else {
  console.log("cold");
}
```

The crucial rule: **only one branch of an `if`/`else if`/`else` chain ever runs.** JavaScript checks conditions from the top, takes the first one that's true, and skips the rest entirely. That "skips the rest" is the reason the original's branch order matters so much (section 3).

Contrast that with **separate** `if` statements:

```js
if (a) { /* might run */ }
if (b) { /* independently might run */ }
```

Here both can run. This distinction — chained versus separate — is the single technical idea at the heart of this project's refactor. If you take one thing from section 2, take this one.

### Boolean operators `&&`, `||`, `!`

```js
a && b   // true only if BOTH are true  ("and")
a || b   // true if EITHER is true       ("or")
!a       // flips true to false          ("not")
```

The original uses `i % 3 == 0 && i % 5 == 0` — "divisible by 3 *and* by 5."

### `for` loops

A `for` loop repeats code a set number of times:

```js
for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
  console.log(i);
}
// prints 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
```

The three parts inside the parentheses, separated by semicolons:

1. **Start:** `let i = 1` — runs once, before anything else.
2. **Keep going while:** `i <= 5` — checked *before* each pass; when it's false, the loop stops.
3. **After each pass:** `i++` — shorthand for `i = i + 1`.

Trace it mentally for `i = 5`: condition `5 <= 5` is true, so the body runs and prints 5; then `i++` makes it 6; then `6 <= 5` is false, so the loop ends. That's why `<=` gives you five iterations and `<` would give you four. Off-by-one errors live in exactly this spot, which is why PRACTICE.md exercise 1 tests the boundaries.

### Functions and return values

A **function** is a named, reusable chunk of code. It can take **inputs** (parameters) and hand back a **result** (`return`):

```js
function double(x) {
  return x * 2;
}

const result = double(21);  // result is 42
```

Three things to internalise:

- `return` **immediately stops** the function and hands the value back.
- A function with no `return` gives back `undefined`.
- Calling a function without using its result is fine — but if the function is pure, it's also pointless.

```js
function noReturn() { const x = 1; }
console.log(noReturn()); // undefined
```

### Pure functions

A **pure function** obeys two rules:

1. Same inputs always produce the same output.
2. It changes nothing outside itself — no printing, no writing files, no modifying global variables.

```js
// PURE — depends only on n, only produces a return value
function fizzbuzz(n) {
  return n % 15 === 0 ? "FizzBuzz" : String(n);
}

// IMPURE — prints (a side effect)
function fizzbuzzPrint(n) {
  console.log(n % 15 === 0 ? "FizzBuzz" : String(n));
}

// IMPURE — different answer every call
function randomNumber() {
  return Math.random();
}

// IMPURE — reaches outside itself
let counter = 0;
function increment() {
  counter++;
}
```

**Why this is the central idea of the repo:** a pure function can be tested by calling it and checking what comes back. That's it. No setup, no fake console, no browser, no database. `assert.equal(fizzbuzz(15), 'FizzBuzz')` is a complete test.

The impure version has no return value to check. To test it you'd have to intercept `console.log` itself — replace the real one with a fake that records what it was asked to print, run the code, inspect the recording, then put the real one back. That's four extra concepts and about fifteen lines of scaffolding, for a program with one line of logic. When testing is that annoying, people don't test. Design caused that.

### Side effects, and why programs need them

A **side effect** is anything a function does besides returning a value: printing, writing a file, sending a network request, drawing on screen.

Here's the point that's easy to miss: side effects aren't bad. A program with no side effects is a program that does nothing observable — it heats up your CPU and tells you nothing. The goal is never to *eliminate* side effects. The goal is to **push them to the edges**, so the middle of your program is pure and testable, and the impure part is small enough to check by eye.

That shape has a name — sometimes "functional core, imperative shell" — and it's what `fizzbuzz.js` (core, pure) plus `cli.js` (shell, prints) is demonstrating in miniature.

### Arrays, `push`, and `join`

An **array** is an ordered list:

```js
const parts = [];        // empty array
parts.push('Fizz');      // add to the end     → ['Fizz']
parts.push('Buzz');      // add another        → ['Fizz', 'Buzz']

console.log(parts.length);  // 2
console.log(parts[0]);      // 'Fizz'  (counting starts at ZERO)
console.log(parts.join('')); // 'FizzBuzz'  (glue with nothing between)
console.log(parts.join('-')); // 'Fizz-Buzz' (glue with a dash)
console.log(parts.join('\n')); // 'Fizz\nBuzz' (glue with newlines)
```

The building-up-an-array pattern (`const x = []`, then `push` in a loop or in `if`s, then `join`) is one of the most useful shapes in JavaScript, and you'll use it in almost every project in this track.

Empty-array edge cases worth memorising, because the refactor depends on them:

```js
[].length      // 0
[].join('')    // ''   — empty string, not undefined, not an error
['Fizz'].join('')  // 'Fizz'  — one element, nothing to glue
```

### The ternary operator `? :`

A one-line `if`/`else` that produces a **value**:

```js
const label = count === 1 ? "item" : "items";

// identical to:
let label;
if (count === 1) { label = "item"; } else { label = "items"; }
```

Read it as: `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`.

Use it for short either/or choices. Don't nest them three deep — that's when it becomes unreadable and a plain `if` is kinder.

### `String(n)`

Converts a value to text:

```js
String(7)     // "7"
String(3.5)   // "3.5"
String(true)  // "true"
```

The refactor uses it so `fizzbuzz()` **always returns a string**, never sometimes a number and sometimes a string. Consistent return types make a function far easier to reason about and to type-check later — and this exact idea is what the whole TypeScript track is about.

You'll also see `n + ''` or `` `${n}` `` used for this. `String(n)` is the clearest, so we use it.

### Template literals

Backtick strings let you embed values:

```js
const n = 3;
console.log(`The answer for ${n} is Fizz`);  // The answer for 3 is Fizz
```

Not used in the FizzBuzz solution, but used constantly in later projects and in test failure messages.

### Modules: `export` and `import`

A **module** is a file that shares code with other files.

```js
// fizzbuzz.js
export function fizzbuzz(n) { /* ... */ }

// cli.js
import { fizzbuzz } from './fizzbuzz.js';
```

Rules that trip people up:

- The `./` is **required** for your own files. `import { x } from 'fizzbuzz.js'` (no dot-slash) makes Node look for an installed package named `fizzbuzz.js` and fail.
- The `.js` extension is **required** in Node's ES modules. Bundlers let you skip it; Node does not.
- This repo's `package.json` contains `"type": "module"`, which is what makes `import`/`export` work in `.js` files at all. Without it you'd get `SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module`.

Modules are how "one file, one job" becomes physically enforceable rather than just a good intention.

### Automated tests, `assert`, and `node:test`

A **test** is code that checks other code:

```js
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { fizzbuzz } from './fizzbuzz.js';

test('multiples of 3 are Fizz', () => {
  assert.equal(fizzbuzz(3), 'Fizz');
});
```

`assert.equal(a, b)` throws an error if `a` and `b` differ. You run all tests with `node --test`, and it prints a pass/fail report. `assert.deepEqual` is the array/object version — it compares *contents*, not just identity.

Why `deepEqual` exists at all:

```js
assert.equal([1,2], [1,2]);      // ❌ FAILS — two different array objects
assert.deepEqual([1,2], [1,2]);  // ✅ passes — same contents
```

`assert/strict` (note the `/strict`) makes `assert.equal` behave like `===` rather than `==`. Always import the strict version.

**Running the tests.** ⚠️ On Node 22 and later, pass a glob, not a folder:

```
node --test "01-fizzbuzz/**/*.test.js"     ✅
node --test 01-fizzbuzz/                    ❌ fails on Node 22+
npm test                                    ✅ runs everything in the repo
```

### The arrow function `() => { }`

You'll see this shape everywhere in test files:

```js
test('a name', () => {
  // the test body
});
```

`() => { ... }` is a compact way to write a function with no name. Here it's a chunk of code handed to `test` so that `test` can run it later, catch any error it throws, and report pass or fail. You don't need to understand arrow functions deeply yet — just recognise the shape as "here is some code to run later."

---

## 3. Walking through the original code

Open `01-fizzbuzz/original.js`. It's fourteen lines. Read it once yourself before reading this.

The whole original is one loop:

```js
for (var i = 1; i <= 100; i++) {
```

Count `i` from 1 up to 100, one step at a time. (Note it uses `var` — remember, that's the leaky old keyword.)

```js
  if (i % 3 == 0 && i % 5 == 0) {
    console.log("FizzBuzz");
```

`&&` means "and". So: if `i` divides evenly by 3 AND by 5, print `FizzBuzz`. This case has to come *first* — if the "divisible by 3" check ran first, 15 would print `Fizz` and never reach here.

```js
  } else if (i % 3 == 0) {
    console.log("Fizz");
  } else if (i % 5 == 0) {
    console.log("Buzz");
```

Otherwise, check the single rules one at a time and print the matching word.

```js
  } else {
    console.log(i);
  }
}
```

If no rule matched, print the number itself. That's it — correct output, 100 lines printed.

### Tracing it by hand

The most valuable thing you can do with a small program is execute it in your head and write down what happens. Here are the first fifteen passes:

| `i` | `i % 3 == 0` | `i % 5 == 0` | Branch taken | Printed |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | false | false | `else` | `1` |
| 2 | false | false | `else` | `2` |
| 3 | **true** | false | 2nd (`else if`) | `Fizz` |
| 4 | false | false | `else` | `4` |
| 5 | false | **true** | 3rd (`else if`) | `Buzz` |
| 6 | **true** | false | 2nd | `Fizz` |
| 7 | false | false | `else` | `7` |
| 8 | false | false | `else` | `8` |
| 9 | **true** | false | 2nd | `Fizz` |
| 10 | false | **true** | 3rd | `Buzz` |
| 11 | false | false | `else` | `11` |
| 12 | **true** | false | 2nd | `Fizz` |
| 13 | false | false | `else` | `13` |
| 14 | false | false | `else` | `14` |
| 15 | **true** | **true** | **1st** | `FizzBuzz` |

Notice row 15. It's the only row in fifteen that reaches the first branch. That's a hint about something important: the first branch is the rarest case, but it's the one that has to be written first, and it's the one that duplicates the other two. The structure is upside-down relative to how often each case actually happens.

### Why the branch order is load-bearing

Try mentally deleting the first branch's priority — reorder to put the `% 3` check first:

```js
if (i % 3 == 0) {           // 15 matches HERE
  console.log("Fizz");
} else if (i % 3 == 0 && i % 5 == 0) {
  console.log("FizzBuzz");  // unreachable for 15 — we already left
}
```

Now 15 prints `Fizz`. The bug isn't in any single line — every line is individually correct. The bug is in the *relationship between* the lines. That's the worst kind of bug: invisible in a code review that reads line by line, and invisible to a reader who doesn't already know the trap.

Hold onto this. Section 6 shows a version where the order genuinely doesn't matter, and that's not a stylistic preference — it's one entire class of bug deleted.

### What runs when you type the command

```
node 01-fizzbuzz/original.js
```

Node reads the file top to bottom, executes the loop 100 times, and each `console.log` writes a line to your terminal's standard output. Then the program ends. There is nothing left over: no value, no function you could call, no way for another program to use any of this. The output went to your eyeballs and nowhere else.

That last sentence is the whole problem, stated as a fact rather than a criticism.

---

## 4. What's wrong with it (in beginner terms)

Remember: the original is **not broken**. It prints exactly the right 100 lines. Everything below is about how hard it is to *change*, which is a different question from whether it works — and, over the life of real software, a much more expensive one.

**1. You can't test it.** Every branch ends in `console.log` — the code *decides* and *prints* in the same breath. There is no function you can call and no return value you can check. The only way to verify it is to run it and read 100 lines with your own eyes. Here's how that bites you: imagine your teammate "optimizes" the loop next month and accidentally makes 15 print `Fizz`. Nothing fails. No alarm rings. The bug ships, because eyeballs were the only test and nobody re-read line 15.

And consider the arithmetic of eyeball-testing. To check this program properly you read 100 lines. Change one character, and to be sure you read 100 lines again. A human reading 100 lines carefully takes a minute or two and gets it wrong sometimes, especially the fifth time, especially at 6pm. The test suite in `refactored/` checks the same thing in 40 milliseconds and is never tired. That's not a small improvement; it's a different category of activity.

**2. `var` leaks.** After the loop ends, `i` still exists and equals 101. In a 15-line file, harmless. In a 500-line file, some *other* code accidentally reads or overwrites that leftover `i`, and you spend an evening finding out why. `let` makes the variable exist only inside the loop, so the mistake becomes impossible.

**3. `==` lies to you.** `"3" == 3` is `true`. Today the loop only compares numbers to numbers, so nothing breaks. But the day this code starts receiving input from a text box or a file (which arrives as *strings*), `==` will quietly "work" by coercion and hide a type bug. `===` would have exposed it immediately.

**4. The combined branch is duplication.** `i % 3 == 0 && i % 5 == 0` re-states the 3-rule and the 5-rule. Now imagine the boss says: "also print `Bazz` for multiples of 7." With this branch style you need branches for 3+5+7, 3+5, 3+7, 5+7, 3, 5, 7, and none — **8 branches for 3 rules**, and 16 for 4 rules. It doubles every time. That's the "combination explosion" the README mentions.

### Doing the explosion arithmetic

It's worth seeing the growth written out, because "it doubles" is abstract until you count it.

| Rules | Branches needed | What that looks like |
|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | 2 | `Fizz`, number |
| 2 | 4 | `FizzBuzz`, `Fizz`, `Buzz`, number |
| 3 | 8 | + `FizzBazz`, `BuzzBazz`, `FizzBuzzBazz`, `Bazz` |
| 4 | 16 | you are now maintaining sixteen branches |
| 5 | 32 | nobody does this |

The formula is 2ⁿ. Meanwhile, the refactored version needs **n** lines for n rules: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Exponential versus linear. For a change as ordinary as "add another rule," one design costs you double every time and the other costs you one line.

This is the moment to notice what "good design" actually means in practice. It is not about elegance or taste. It's about which changes are cheap. The refactor makes exactly one kind of change cheap — adding a rule — because that's the change this program is realistically going to get asked for.

### The cost table

| Change requested | Cost in `original.js` | Cost in `refactored/` |
|---|---|---|
| Add a `Bazz` rule for 7 | Rewrite the branch tree: 4 branches → 8 | One line |
| Print 1–15 instead of 1–100 | Edit the loop; re-read output by eye to verify | Edit `cli.js`; zero tests break |
| Use the result in a web page instead of a terminal | Rewrite everything — the logic is welded to `console.log` | `import { fizzbuzz }`, done |
| Prove 15 still says FizzBuzz after an edit | Read 100 lines of output | `npm test`, 40ms |
| Count how many Fizzes there are | Can't — the data doesn't exist anywhere | `fizzbuzzRange(1,100).filter(...)` |

That last row is the one that surprises people. In the original, the sequence never exists as *data* — each line is computed and immediately thrown at the terminal. There is no moment where the program is holding the answer. So any question about the answer as a whole ("how many?", "what's the longest?", "give me the first ten") is unanswerable without rewriting. The refactor produces an array, and an array can be counted, filtered, sorted, sliced, and sent anywhere.

**5. It can only ever do one thing.** Related to the above but worth stating separately: `original.js` prints 1 to 100 to a terminal. That's not a feature of the file, it's the *entirety* of the file. It cannot be reused, imported, tested, or repurposed, because it exposes nothing. It's a program-shaped object with no handles on it.

## 6. Understanding the refactored solution

The refactor splits one file into three, each with one job.

```
refactored/
├── fizzbuzz.js       ← the rules. Pure. Never prints.
├── cli.js            ← the printing. Two lines.
└── fizzbuzz.test.js  ← the checks.
```

That three-file shape — logic, entry point, tests — recurs in almost every project in this repo. Getting used to it now pays off eighty-four more times.

**`fizzbuzz.js` — the rules.** Never prints anything.

```js
export function fizzbuzz(n) {
  const parts = [];
  if (n % 3 === 0) parts.push('Fizz');
  if (n % 5 === 0) parts.push('Buzz');
  return parts.length > 0 ? parts.join('') : String(n);
}
```

Line by line:

- `const parts = []` — start with an empty list of word-pieces. `const` is right here even though we're about to change the array, because we never reassign the variable itself.
- `if (n % 3 === 0) parts.push('Fizz');` — an **independent** `if`. No `else`.
- `if (n % 5 === 0) parts.push('Buzz');` — another **independent** `if`. For n = 15, both of these run, and `parts` becomes `['Fizz', 'Buzz']`.
- `parts.join('')` glues them into `'FizzBuzz'` with nothing in between.
- `parts.length > 0 ? ... : String(n)` — if no rule matched, `parts` is empty, so fall back to the number as a string.

**The whole trick is the missing `else`.** That's it. That one absence is what turns four branches into two lines and kills the combination explosion. Adding `Bazz`:

```js
  if (n % 7 === 0) parts.push('Bazz');
```

One line, inserted anywhere among the others, and every combination — `FizzBazz`, `BuzzBazz`, `FizzBuzzBazz` — works automatically, because combinations are now something the *data* does rather than something the *code* enumerates.

Sit with that phrase, because it generalises far beyond FizzBuzz: **the combinations moved from the code into the data.** Code that enumerates cases grows exponentially with the number of cases. Code that accumulates data grows linearly. Whenever you find yourself writing branch after branch for combinations of conditions, this is the move to reach for.

### Why the order of the `if`s doesn't matter (and why that's a big deal)

Swap the two `if` statements:

```js
if (n % 5 === 0) parts.push('Buzz');
if (n % 3 === 0) parts.push('Fizz');
```

Now `fizzbuzz(15)` returns `'BuzzFizz'`. Different output — so order isn't *totally* irrelevant; it controls the sequence of the words. But note what *can't* happen: no rule can ever hide another rule. There is no arrangement of these lines that makes 15 come out as plain `Fizz`.

In the original, order controlled **correctness**. Here, order controls only **presentation**. Demoting a correctness concern to a cosmetic one is a real, permanent reduction in how much you have to keep in your head — and one fewer thing a future reader can get wrong.

### Why `String(n)` and not just `n`

```js
return parts.length > 0 ? parts.join('') : String(n);
//                                          ^^^^^^^^^
```

Without `String()`, this function would return a string sometimes and a number other times. That's a small landmine:

```js
fizzbuzz(3).toUpperCase()   // 'FIZZ' — fine
fizzbuzz(4).toUpperCase()   // 💥 TypeError if it returned the number 4
```

A function whose return type depends on its input is a function every caller has to defend against. Making it always a string costs seven characters and removes an entire class of caller bug. (In the TypeScript track, `typescript/01-any-epidemic` onward, this becomes a compile-time guarantee rather than a discipline.)

**`fizzbuzzRange(start, end)` — the sequence, still as data.**

```js
export function fizzbuzzRange(start, end) {
  const lines = [];
  for (let n = start; n <= end; n++) {
    lines.push(fizzbuzz(n));
  }
  return lines;
}
```

Same pattern one level up: build an array, return it, print nothing. Note `let n` rather than `var i`, and that the range is a **parameter** rather than hard-coded 1 and 100 — so this function can serve a CLI, a test, or a web page without modification.

It returns an array rather than a joined string on purpose. An array is the more useful thing: the caller can join it, count it, filter it, or slice it. If it returned a pre-joined string, a caller who wanted to count the Fizzes would have to split it apart again. **Return the most structured form you have; let the caller flatten it.**

**`cli.js` — the only file that touches the outside world.**

```js
import { fizzbuzzRange } from './fizzbuzz.js';

console.log(fizzbuzzRange(1, 100).join('\n'));
```

Two lines. Everything a bug could hide in has been moved out. There is nothing to test here, and that's the point — the untestable part has been made small enough that "read it once" is genuinely sufficient verification.

Note it does one `console.log` of a joined string rather than 100 separate calls. Slightly faster, and more importantly it makes explicit that the program produces *one* output: a block of text.

### The shape, in one picture

```
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  fizzbuzz.js       PURE — testable      │
     │  ─────────────                          │
     │  fizzbuzz(n)       number → string      │
     │  fizzbuzzRange()   range  → array       │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    ▲               ▲
        imports     │               │    imports
                    │               │
     ┌──────────────┴───┐   ┌───────┴────────────┐
     │  cli.js          │   │  fizzbuzz.test.js  │
     │  IMPURE — prints │   │  the safety net    │
     │  2 lines         │   │                    │
     └──────────────────┘   └────────────────────┘
```

The pure core has no idea it's being printed, and no idea it's being tested. It just answers questions. Both of the things that use it — the CLI and the test suite — are *clients* of the same clean interface. That's why adding a third client (a web page, an HTTP endpoint, another program) costs nothing.

## 7. Designs we considered and rejected

There isn't one right answer, and it's worth understanding the alternatives — partly so you recognise them in other people's code, partly because the reasons *against* them are more instructive than the reason for ours.

### The `n % 15` shortcut

```js
function fizzbuzz(n) {
  if (n % 15 === 0) return 'FizzBuzz';
  if (n % 3 === 0) return 'Fizz';
  if (n % 5 === 0) return 'Buzz';
  return String(n);
}
```

Clever: 15 is 3 × 5, so one check covers both. Shorter than the original and genuinely readable.

**Why not:** it's the combination explosion in disguise. Add `Bazz` for 7 and you need checks for 105, 21, 35, and 15 before the singles — you're back to enumerating combinations, now with magic numbers whose meaning isn't visible. The `15` also silently encodes "3 and 5 are coprime," a fact that isn't true for every pair of rules you might add (try 4 and 6). It optimises for the version of the problem that never changes.

### String concatenation instead of an array

```js
function fizzbuzz(n) {
  let out = '';
  if (n % 3 === 0) out += 'Fizz';
  if (n % 5 === 0) out += 'Buzz';
  return out || String(n);
}
```

Honestly, this is fine. It's the same design — independent `if`s, accumulate, fall back — with a string as the accumulator instead of an array. `out || String(n)` works because `''` is falsy.

**Why we chose the array anyway:** two small reasons. First, `parts.length > 0` says what it means more plainly than relying on the reader knowing that empty strings are falsy. Second, an array keeps the pieces *separate* until the last moment, which matters the instant someone wants `'Fizz-Buzz'` or `['Fizz','Buzz']` instead — a change that's one argument to `join` here and a rewrite there. Keeping data structured for as long as possible is a habit worth building.

### A lookup table

```js
const RULES = [
  [3, 'Fizz'],
  [5, 'Buzz'],
];

function fizzbuzz(n) {
  const parts = RULES
    .filter(([divisor]) => n % divisor === 0)
    .map(([, word]) => word);
  return parts.length > 0 ? parts.join('') : String(n);
}
```

This is arguably the *best* design, and PRACTICE.md exercise 4 walks you to it. Adding a rule is now editing **data**, not code — and data can come from a config file, a user, or a database. It also makes the rules inspectable: another function can read `RULES` and describe them.

**Why it isn't the shipped version:** it needs `filter`, `map`, array destructuring, and array-of-arrays — four concepts, in project 01, before you've met any of them. The shipped refactor teaches the one idea that matters (independent `if`s, accumulate) with the smallest possible vocabulary. Project 10 (`10-rpn-calculator`) and project 13 (`13-cipher-suite`) return to data-driven dispatch once you have the tools for it.

This is itself a design lesson: **the best design for a codebase and the best design for a teaching example are not always the same,** and neither is the "most advanced" one. Match the tool to the audience.

### A `switch` statement

```js
switch (true) {
  case n % 15 === 0: return 'FizzBuzz';
  case n % 3 === 0: return 'Fizz';
  // ...
}
```

`switch (true)` is a trick for using `switch` with arbitrary conditions. It works, but it's unfamiliar enough that most readers stop and squint, and it has all the problems of the `% 15` version. `switch` earns its place when you're matching one value against many constants — see `06-rock-paper-scissors` and `typescript/12-exhaustive-switch` for where it genuinely shines.

### Printing inside the function

```js
function fizzbuzz(n) {
  console.log(/* ... */);
}
```

This is the original's design with a function wrapped around it. It looks like progress — there's a function now! — but it isn't, because the function still can't be tested: there's no return value. **A function is not automatically an improvement. Extracting logic only helps if you also extract the *decision*, not just the code.**

Watch for this one. It's the most common half-refactor, and it feels productive.

## 8. How the test file works

Open `refactored/fizzbuzz.test.js`. It's short, and it's the template for every test you'll write in this track.

```js
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { fizzbuzz, fizzbuzzRange } from './fizzbuzz.js';
```

Three imports: the test runner built into Node, the strict assertion library, and the code being tested. No packages installed, no config file, no framework. This is a real advantage of Node's built-in runner and part of why this repo has almost no dependencies.

```js
test('multiples of both are FizzBuzz', () => {
  assert.equal(fizzbuzz(15), 'FizzBuzz');
  assert.equal(fizzbuzz(45), 'FizzBuzz');
});
```

Each `test(...)` takes a **name** and a **function**. The runner calls the function; if it throws, the test fails, and if it returns quietly, the test passes. That's the entire mechanism. `assert.equal` throws when the values differ. Nothing magic is happening.

### Reading a failure

Deliberately break something — change `n % 3` to `n % 4` in `fizzbuzz.js` — and run the tests. You'll see something like:

```
✖ multiples of 3 are Fizz (1.2ms)
  AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: Expected values to be strictly equal:
+ actual - expected

+ '3'
- 'Fizz'
        at TestContext.<anonymous> (fizzbuzz.test.js:12:10)
```

Four things to read, in order:

1. **The test name** — `multiples of 3 are Fizz`. This is why test names should describe behaviour, not mechanics. `test('test1')` tells you nothing here.
2. **`+ actual` / `- expected`** — what you got versus what you wanted. Actual `'3'`, expected `'Fizz'`.
3. **The file and line** — `fizzbuzz.test.js:12:10` — which assertion blew up.
4. **The summary at the bottom** — how many passed and failed overall.

Getting comfortable reading these is a genuine skill, and the fastest way to build it is to break things on purpose. Experiment 2 in section 13 asks you to do exactly that.

### Why these five tests, and not fifty

The test file checks: a plain number, a multiple of 3, a multiple of 5, a multiple of both, and the range function. Five tests, and they were chosen rather than accumulated.

Good tests cover **categories of behaviour**, not individual values. There's no point testing 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 21… — they all exercise the same line of code. One representative per category, plus the boundaries and the awkward cases, is the standard to aim for. Two per category (the file uses 3 and 9, 5 and 20) is cheap insurance against a test that passes by coincidence.

What's arguably **missing**: what should `fizzbuzz(0)` do? What about negatives, or `1.5`, or `"15"`? The current code has answers for all of those, but nobody decided them on purpose — they're accidents of the implementation. PRACTICE.md exercise 1 is about noticing that untested behaviour is undecided behaviour.

## 9. Where this actually shows up in real software

FizzBuzz is a toy. The pattern isn't. Some places the exact same split appears at full scale:

- **A web server.** The impure shell reads an HTTP request and writes a response. The pure core takes a plain object of parameters and returns a plain object of results. You can then test every rule your business has without starting a server or making a request. Project `65-rest-api` builds this.
- **A React component.** The impure shell renders to the DOM; the pure core is a reducer — `(state, action) => newState` — that decides what should happen. Testing a reducer needs no browser. `react/13-usereducer-todo` and `react/40-undo-redo` are FizzBuzz with more state.
- **A game loop.** The impure shell reads the keyboard and draws to canvas; the pure core is `step(state) => nextState`. Project `17-snake` is exactly this, and the reason its logic is pure is the reason you can test whether the snake dies on a wall without pressing an arrow key.
- **A compiler or parser.** Text in, structured data out, nothing printed. Projects `69-json-parser`, `70-pratt-calculator`, and `71-tiny-lang` are all one enormous pure function with a thin CLI.
- **A pricing or billing engine.** The rules ("apply this discount if…") are pure and heavily tested because they're where money lives; the database and the invoice PDF are the shell. Project `32-money-cart`.

In every one of these, the question that drives the design is the one from section 1: *how would I test this?* And the answer is always the same move — pull the deciding out of the doing.

### The counter-argument, honestly stated

Is this always right? No. For a genuine fourteen-line throwaway script that you'll run once and delete, three files and a test suite is worse than one file. Ceremony has a cost, and applying heavyweight structure to trivial code is its own failure mode — you'll meet the opposite lesson in project `04-caesar-solver` ("generalize when you need it") and again in `26-array-utils`.

The judgement call is: **is this going to be read or changed again?** If yes — and in professional work the answer is almost always yes, by someone who isn't you, later than you think — the split pays for itself the first time somebody has to change it. If genuinely no, write the fourteen lines and move on.

What makes FizzBuzz a good teacher is that it's small enough to see both sides of that argument at once.

## 10. Mistakes people actually make here

Real error messages and what they mean.

**`SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module`**
You ran a file with `import` in it, but Node didn't know it's a module. This repo's root `package.json` has `"type": "module"`, so this only happens if you copied a file somewhere outside the repo. Fix: keep your scratch files inside the repo, or rename yours to `.mjs`.

**`Error: Cannot find module '/path/to/fizzbuzz'`**
You wrote `import { fizzbuzz } from './fizzbuzz'` without the `.js`. Node requires the extension. Add it.

**`ReferenceError: fizzbuzz is not defined`**
Either you forgot the `import`, or you forgot `export` on the function, or the names don't match. The braces matter: `import { fizzbuzz }` requires `export function fizzbuzz`. A typo in either name gives you this.

**`# tests 1 · pass 0 · fail 1` with `Cannot find module '...\01-fizzbuzz'`**
You ran `node --test 01-fizzbuzz/`. On Node 22+ a bare directory is treated as a module to load, not a folder to scan. Use `node --test "01-fizzbuzz/**/*.test.js"` or just `npm test`.

**`fizzbuzz(15)` returns `'Fizz'`**
You used `else if` between the two rules. This is *the* mistake this project teaches. Make them two independent statements.

**`fizzbuzz(15)` returns `'BuzzFizz'`**
Your `if`s are in the other order. Not a bug in any strict sense — but conventionally Fizz comes first, and the test asserts that. Worth noticing that the test is enforcing a *convention* here, not a correctness property.

**`TypeError: parts.join is not a function`**
You wrote `const parts = ''` (a string) but then called an array method on it. Strings have `concat`, arrays have `join`.

**`TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.`**
You wrote `parts = [...]` somewhere instead of `parts.push(...)`. `const` forbids reassigning the box; pushing into the array is fine.

**Tests pass but the CLI prints nothing**
Check that `cli.js` actually calls `console.log`, and that you ran `node 01-fizzbuzz/refactored/cli.js` rather than `fizzbuzz.js`. Running `fizzbuzz.js` directly is *supposed* to print nothing — it only defines functions. That's not a bug, it's the design.

## 12. Words you learned (glossary)

- **Variable** — a named box holding a value.
- **Value** — a piece of data: a number, a string, a boolean, an array.
- **Type** — the kind of a value (`number`, `string`, `boolean`, `object`). `typeof x` tells you.
- **Block scope** — a variable existing only inside its `{ }` braces (`let`/`const` do this; `var` doesn't).
- **Reassignment** — pointing an existing variable at a new value. `const` forbids it; mutating an array's *contents* is not reassignment.
- **`%` (modulo/remainder)** — remainder after division; `n % 3 === 0` means "n is a multiple of 3."
- **Type coercion** — JavaScript auto-converting one type to another, as `==` does.
- **Strict equality (`===`)** — comparison with no conversion; use it always.
- **Truthy / falsy** — values that behave like `true`/`false` in a condition. Falsy: `false`, `0`, `''`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. Everything else is truthy.
- **Branch** — one path through an `if`/`else` chain.
- **Function** — reusable chunk of code that can take inputs and `return` a result.
- **Parameter** — a function's named input.
- **Argument** — the actual value you pass in when calling it.
- **Return value** — the answer a function hands back to its caller.
- **Pure function** — same input → same output, with no side effects (no printing, no changing outside state).
- **Side effect** — anything a function does besides returning a value (printing, writing files, etc.).
- **Functional core, imperative shell** — the shape where pure logic sits in the middle and side effects are pushed to a thin outer layer.
- **Array** — an ordered list of values; `push` adds, `join` glues into a string, `length` counts.
- **Index** — an item's position in an array, counting from **zero**.
- **Accumulator** — a variable you build up piece by piece in a loop (`parts` here).
- **Ternary (`? :`)** — one-line if/else that produces a value.
- **Template literal** — a backtick string with `${}` holes for values.
- **Module** — a file that `export`s code for other files to `import`.
- **Named export** — `export function foo`, imported with braces: `import { foo }`.
- **CLI** — command-line interface; the thin file you run in a terminal.
- **Entry point** — the file you actually run (`cli.js` here).
- **Test** — code that automatically checks other code.
- **Assertion** — a single check inside a test.
- **`assert`** — a check that throws an error when a value isn't what you expected.
- **Test runner** — the tool that finds tests, runs them, and reports results (`node --test`).
- **Regression** — a bug introduced by a change that used to work. Tests exist mostly to catch these.
- **Combination explosion** — the 2ⁿ growth in branches when you enumerate combinations of conditions instead of accumulating them.
- **Magic number** — an unexplained literal in code (the `15` in the `n % 15` variant).
- **Refactor** — changing a program's structure without changing its behaviour.
- **`\n`** — the newline character.

7. **Swap the rule order.** Put the `% 5` check first. Predict the output for 15. Expected: `'BuzzFizz'`, and the FizzBuzz test fails. Now ask: is the code *wrong*, or is the test enforcing a convention? (Both readings are defensible — that's the interesting part.)

## Solutions

Read these *after* attempting. The WHY paragraphs are the part worth your time.

### 1. Edge-of-range tests

```js
test('a single-number range has one entry', () => {
  assert.deepEqual(fizzbuzzRange(15, 15), ['FizzBuzz']);
});

test('a backwards range is empty', () => {
  assert.deepEqual(fizzbuzzRange(5, 1), []);
});
```

**WHY:** the loop condition `n <= end` is false immediately when start > end, so the array stays empty — no crash, no special case needed. Writing that down as a test turns an accident of the implementation into a documented promise. This is the project's core idea: pure functions make checking behaviour a one-liner.

The distinction between *accident* and *promise* is worth dwelling on. Before you wrote this test, `fizzbuzzRange(5,1) === []` was true but nobody had decided it should be — a future contributor could "fix" it to throw, or to count downward, and nothing would object. After the test, it's a commitment. Tests are the only place in a codebase where intent is unambiguous, because code shows what happens and comments go stale, but a failing test stops the build.

Note also that `assert.deepEqual` is required here. `assert.equal([], [])` **fails**, because those are two distinct array objects and strict equality compares identity, not contents.

### 2. fizzbuzzStats

```js
export function fizzbuzzStats(start, end) {
  const stats = { fizz: 0, buzz: 0, fizzbuzz: 0, plain: 0 };
  for (let n = start; n <= end; n++) {
    const result = fizzbuzz(n);
    if (result === 'Fizz') stats.fizz++;
    else if (result === 'Buzz') stats.buzz++;
    else if (result === 'FizzBuzz') stats.fizzbuzz++;
    else stats.plain++;
  }
  return stats;
}
```

**WHY:** because `fizzbuzz` *returns* its answer, other code can build on it — the stats function never repeats the `% 3` / `% 5` rules, so if the rules ever change, stats stays correct for free. Verified by running: 1–15 gives `{fizz:4, buzz:2, fizzbuzz:1, plain:8}` and 1–100 gives `{fizz:27, buzz:14, fizzbuzz:6, plain:53}`.

Two details worth noticing. First, this is a legitimate use of `else if` — these four outcomes really are mutually exclusive, because a single string can't equal two different values. The refactor's lesson isn't "`else if` is bad"; it's "`else if` is wrong when the cases *aren't* exclusive." Knowing which situation you're in is the actual skill.

Second, `stats` is `const` yet we mutate it with `stats.fizz++` throughout — same rule as `const parts = []`. `const` protects the binding, not the contents.

**A variation to consider:** if you added `Bazz` for 7, this function breaks — everything lands in `plain`. A more robust version counts by the returned string itself:

```js
export function fizzbuzzTally(start, end) {
  const tally = {};
  for (let n = start; n <= end; n++) {
    const key = fizzbuzz(n);
    tally[key] = (tally[key] ?? 0) + 1;
  }
  return tally;
}
```

That counts every distinct output including each individual number, which is a different and often less useful answer — so the "right" version depends on the question you're asking. Neither is wrong; be clear which you meant.

### 3. run-range.js

```js
import { fizzbuzzRange } from './fizzbuzz.js';

const start = Number(process.argv[2] ?? 1);
const end = Number(process.argv[3] ?? 100);
console.log(fizzbuzzRange(start, end).join('\n'));
```

**WHY:** the rules file didn't change at all — only the thin I/O layer grew by two lines. That's the README's point about `cli.js` being "too simple to contain bugs": argument parsing stays in the disposable outer shell, and `node --test` still passes untouched.

`process.argv` is worth understanding properly. It's an array where `[0]` is the path to Node itself, `[1]` is the path to your script, and everything from `[2]` on is what the user typed. So `node run-range.js 14 16` gives you `['...node', '...run-range.js', '14', '16']`.

Both of those are **strings**. `Number('14')` converts, and `Number(undefined)` is `NaN` — which is why the `?? 1` default is applied *before* `Number()`, not after. Try writing it the other way round and see what `node run-range.js` alone does. (`NaN <= NaN` is false, so the loop never runs and you get one empty line.) That ordering bug is small, silent, and extremely common.

If you did exercise 10 as well, note that validation now catches this class of mistake loudly instead.

### 4. fizzbuzzWith

```js
export function fizzbuzzWith(n, rules) {
  const parts = [];
  for (const [divisor, word] of rules) {
    if (n % divisor === 0) parts.push(word);
  }
  return parts.length > 0 ? parts.join('') : String(n);
}
```

Test that the classic game is a special case:

```js
test('fizzbuzz is fizzbuzzWith with the classic rules', () => {
  const CLASSIC = [[3, 'Fizz'], [5, 'Buzz']];
  for (let n = 1; n <= 100; n++) {
    assert.equal(fizzbuzzWith(n, CLASSIC), fizzbuzz(n));
  }
  assert.equal(fizzbuzzWith(21, [[3, 'Fizz'], [7, 'Bazz']]), 'FizzBazz');
});
```

**WHY:** the "build up parts" pattern already treated each rule independently, so turning the rule list into a parameter is a five-line change — the combination explosion never comes back no matter how many rules the caller passes. This is exactly the generalization project 04 performs on the Caesar cipher, practised a project early.

The `for (const [divisor, word] of rules)` line does two things at once: `for...of` walks the array, and `[divisor, word]` **destructures** each inner pair into two named variables. Without destructuring you'd write `rule[0]` and `rule[1]`, which works and is meaningfully worse — the names are the documentation.

And once you have `fizzbuzzWith`, the original becomes:

```js
export const CLASSIC_RULES = [[3, 'Fizz'], [5, 'Buzz']];
export const fizzbuzz = (n) => fizzbuzzWith(n, CLASSIC_RULES);
```

All five original tests pass unchanged. That's the signature of a good generalization: the specific case survives as a one-line application of the general one, and its tests don't notice. If your generalization forces you to rewrite the existing tests, it changed behaviour — that's a different and more dangerous kind of change.

**The honest caveat.** Should the shipped `fizzbuzz.js` be written this way? For a repo teaching project 01, no — as LEARN.md section 7 argues, it needs four concepts you haven't met yet. Generalizing before you have a second use case is also its own failure mode, and project 04 is entirely about when to resist that urge. Here you have a second use case (`Bazz`), so it's earned.

### 5. Property test

```js
test('FizzBuzz appears exactly for multiples of 15', () => {
  for (let n = 1; n <= 300; n++) {
    assert.equal(fizzbuzz(n) === 'FizzBuzz', n % 15 === 0);
  }
});
```

**WHY:** example tests check points; property tests check a *shape*. The `===` on the left and the `% 15` on the right are both booleans, so the assert says "these two facts must always agree" — sabotage either rule in `fizzbuzz` and some n in 1..300 exposes it. Compare with project 03's "rot13 is its own inverse" test: same idea.

The two extra properties from "going further":

```js
test('every result is a non-empty string', () => {
  for (let n = 1; n <= 300; n++) {
    const r = fizzbuzz(n);
    assert.equal(typeof r, 'string');
    assert.ok(r.length > 0, `empty result for ${n}`);
  }
});

test('Fizz appears exactly for multiples of 3', () => {
  for (let n = 1; n <= 300; n++) {
    assert.equal(fizzbuzz(n).includes('Fizz'), n % 3 === 0);
  }
});
```

Note the third argument to `assert.ok` — a message shown when it fails, with the offending `n` interpolated. In a 300-iteration loop that message is the difference between a two-second diagnosis and a ten-minute one. Always include it in loop assertions.

Note also the shift from `===` to `.includes()` in the last one. `fizzbuzz(15)` doesn't *equal* `'Fizz'`, but it does *contain* it — and "contains Fizz iff divisible by 3" is the property that stays true no matter how many other rules exist. Properties that survive future changes are more valuable than properties that don't, and choosing between `===` and `includes` here is exactly that judgement.

Real property-based testing libraries (fast-check, and QuickCheck in other languages) generate random inputs and shrink failures to a minimal example. This hand-rolled loop is the same idea with a fixed input set — enough to get most of the benefit with zero dependencies.

### 6. firstMatches

```js
export function firstMatches(word, count, limit = 100000) {
  const matches = [];
  for (let n = 1; matches.length < count && n <= limit; n++) {
    if (fizzbuzz(n) === word) matches.push(n);
  }
  return matches;
}
```

**WHY:** the loop condition encodes both "am I done?" and "have I searched long enough?" — without the limit, `firstMatches('Qux', 1)` would spin forever because no number ever produces `'Qux'`. Verified by running: `('FizzBuzz', 3)` → `[15, 30, 45]`, `('Buzz', 4)` → `[5, 10, 20, 25]`, `('Qux', 2)` → `[]`. Returning data (an array) keeps it as testable as everything else in this project.

The `limit = 100000` default parameter is doing real design work. Hard-coding the number inside the function would make the safety valve untestable — you'd need a hundred thousand iterations to prove it engages. As a parameter, a test can pass `limit = 20` and check the behaviour instantly:

```js
test('gives up at the limit', () => {
  assert.deepEqual(firstMatches('Qux', 5, 20), []);
  assert.deepEqual(firstMatches('Fizz', 5, 10), [3, 6, 9]);  // ran out of room
});
```

That second case is the more interesting one: it returns *partial* results rather than throwing. Whether that's right depends on the caller — a search UI wants partial results, a correctness-critical batch job probably wants an error. Both are defensible; what's not defensible is not having decided, which is exactly the trap exercise 10 is about.

`firstMatches('FizzBuzz', 0)` returning `[]` falls out for free: `matches.length < count` is `0 < 0`, false, so the loop never starts. Edge cases that require no special-casing are a sign the loop condition is expressing the right idea.

### 7. Return type test

```js
test('every line is a string, including plain numbers', () => {
  const lines = fizzbuzzRange(1, 100);
  assert.ok(lines.every((line) => typeof line === 'string'));
});
```

**WHY:** `String(n)` in the implementation is a *promise* that this function's output type never varies. Untested promises get broken during refactors by people who don't know the promise exists. Four lines makes it enforceable.

`.every()` returns `true` only if the callback returns truthy for every element — it's the array version of "for all." Its partner is `.some()` ("there exists"). Both short-circuit, so `.every` stops at the first failure.

For a better failure message, loop instead:

```js
for (const [i, line] of fizzbuzzRange(1, 100).entries()) {
  assert.equal(typeof line, 'string', `index ${i} was ${typeof line}`);
}
```

`.every()` tells you *that* something failed; the loop tells you *which*. Prefer the loop when the collection is large enough that "which" is hard to find by hand.

**The deeper point:** this whole exercise exists because JavaScript won't check it for you. In the TypeScript track, `function fizzbuzz(n: number): string` makes this test unnecessary — the compiler refuses to build code that could return a number. That's the entire argument of `typescript/01-any-epidemic` onward: some tests are better expressed as types, because a type checks *every* call site rather than the ones you thought to test.

### 8. Generator version

```js
export function* fizzbuzzSeq(start, end) {
  for (let n = start; n <= end; n++) {
    yield fizzbuzz(n);
  }
}

export function fizzbuzzRange(start, end) {
  return [...fizzbuzzSeq(start, end)];
}
```

**WHY:** `function*` declares a generator; `yield` hands one value to whoever is iterating and **pauses** until they ask for the next. Nothing is computed until it's asked for, and nothing is retained after it's consumed.

Calling `fizzbuzzSeq(1, 5)` runs *zero* lines of the body — it returns an iterator. The body only advances when something pulls: a `for...of`, a spread `[...]`, or a manual `.next()`. That inversion of control ("the consumer sets the pace") is what makes generators useful for streams, infinite sequences, and anything too large to materialise.

All five original tests pass unchanged, because `fizzbuzzRange` still returns an array with the same contents. The internals changed completely and the interface didn't — which is the definition of a refactor, and the reason the tests were worth writing.

Watch the memory difference concretely:

```js
fizzbuzzRange(1, 10_000_000)   // builds a 10M-element array first
for (const line of fizzbuzzSeq(1, 10_000_000)) { /* one at a time */ }
```

The first can exhaust memory; the second is constant-space. Project 85 (`85-streaming-log-parser`) is this idea applied to a file you can't fit in RAM, and project 22 (`22-ulam-spiral`) uses it for a genuinely infinite sequence — a generator can yield forever, which an array obviously cannot.

### 9. Injectable output

```js
// cli.js
import { fizzbuzzRange } from './fizzbuzz.js';

export function main(out = console.log) {
  out(fizzbuzzRange(1, 100).join('\n'));
}

main();
```

```js
// cli.test.js
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { main } from './cli.js';

test('main prints 100 lines', () => {
  const printed = [];
  main((s) => printed.push(s));

  assert.equal(printed.length, 1);
  assert.equal(printed[0].split('\n').length, 100);
  assert.equal(printed[0].split('\n')[14], 'FizzBuzz');
});
```

**WHY:** the side effect became a **parameter**. In production nobody passes anything, so the default `console.log` is used and behaviour is unchanged. In a test you pass a recorder and inspect what would have been printed. This technique — dependency injection — is how every untestable thing becomes testable: the clock, the filesystem, the network, randomness, the database.

The general shape is always the same. Find the thing that talks to the outside world, make it an argument, give it a sensible default. Compare:

```js
function greet()            { console.log('hi'); }      // untestable
function greet(out = console.log) { out('hi'); }        // testable, same to callers

function expire()           { return Date.now() > t; }  // untestable
function expire(now = Date.now) { return now() > t; }   // testable

function pick(a)            { return a[Math.floor(Math.random()*a.length)]; }
function pick(a, rand = Math.random) { return a[Math.floor(rand()*a.length)]; }
```

That last one is exactly how `11-password-generator` and `18-yahtzee` make randomness testable: pass a fake `rand` that returns a fixed sequence, and dice rolls become deterministic. Project 43 (`43-retry-timeout`) does it with timers, and `react/22-custom-hook-usefetch` does it with `fetch`.

**One caveat, since `main()` runs at import time:** the test file importing `cli.js` will trigger that bare `main()` call and print 100 lines into your test output. Guard it if that annoys you:

```js
if (import.meta.url === `file://${process.argv[1]}`) main();
```

That's the ES-module version of "only run when executed directly, not when imported" — the same idea as Python's `if __name__ == "__main__"`.

### 10. Input validation

```js
function assertInteger(name, value) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(value)) {
    throw new RangeError(`${name} must be an integer, got ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
  }
}

export function fizzbuzzRange(start, end) {
  assertInteger('start', start);
  assertInteger('end', end);

  const lines = [];
  for (let n = start; n <= end; n++) lines.push(fizzbuzz(n));
  return lines;
}
```

```js
test('rejects non-integer bounds', () => {
  assert.throws(() => fizzbuzzRange('a', 5), /start must be an integer/);
  assert.throws(() => fizzbuzzRange(1, Infinity), /end must be an integer/);
  assert.throws(() => fizzbuzzRange(1.5, 5), /start must be an integer/);
});

test('a backwards range is still allowed', () => {
  assert.deepEqual(fizzbuzzRange(5, 1), []);
});
```

**WHY:** `Number.isInteger` rejects `NaN`, `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, `1.5`, and every string in a single check — far better than a hand-rolled chain of `typeof` and `isNaN`. Note it's `Number.isInteger`, not the global `isInteger`, and definitely not the global `isNaN`, which coerces its argument and will tell you `isNaN('')` is `false`.

Three things the error message does deliberately: it names *which* parameter was wrong, states what was expected, and shows what actually arrived. An error saying only `"Invalid input"` costs the next person twenty minutes. `JSON.stringify` around the value is a small touch that makes `'a'` visibly a string rather than an unquoted mystery.

`assert.throws(fn, /regex/)` takes a *function* — note the `() =>` wrapper. Passing `fizzbuzzRange('a', 5)` directly would call it, throw immediately, and fail the test before `assert.throws` ever ran. Forgetting the arrow is the classic mistake with this assertion.

`RangeError` rather than a plain `Error` because JavaScript has built-in error types that carry meaning, and callers can catch selectively. Project 30 (`30-custom-errors`) takes this further with error classes of your own.

**And notice what we did *not* validate:** a backwards range still returns `[]`, because exercise 1 established that as intended behaviour. Validation should reject what's genuinely meaningless, not everything unusual. Over-validating is its own bug — it turns working code into a crash.

### 11. Table-driven tests

```js
const CASES = [
  [1, '1'],
  [2, '2'],
  [3, 'Fizz'],
  [5, 'Buzz'],
  [9, 'Fizz'],
  [15, 'FizzBuzz'],
  [20, 'Buzz'],
  [45, 'FizzBuzz'],
  [100, 'Buzz'],
];

for (const [input, expected] of CASES) {
  test(`fizzbuzz(${input}) === '${expected}'`, () => {
    assert.equal(fizzbuzz(input), expected);
  });
}
```

**WHY:** adding a case is adding a row. The test *name* is generated from the data, so the runner still reports nine separate results and a failure names the exact input — you get the table's brevity without losing per-case reporting.

The critical detail is that `test()` is called **inside** the loop, not around it. Get it backwards:

```js
test('all cases', () => {              // ⚠️ one test, not nine
  for (const [input, expected] of CASES) {
    assert.equal(fizzbuzz(input), expected);
  }
});
```

and the first failure aborts the loop, hiding every later failure. When you're mid-refactor and six things are broken, "one failure" versus "six failures" is the difference between six debugging cycles and one.

**The honest trade-off,** as flagged in the exercise: this is a win when cases are uniform and numerous. It's a loss when they aren't — the moment one case needs different setup, the table sprouts an options column, then a skip flag, then a callback, and you've built a small unreadable framework. The name for that failure is "test DSL," and it's a real cost. Nine uniform rows is comfortably on the good side of the line. Ninety would be clearly good. Three would not be worth it.

### 12. Mutation testing

Results for each sabotage:

| Mutation | Tests that fail | Caught? |
|---|---|---|
| `else if` between the two rules | `multiples of both are FizzBuzz` | ✅ |
| `parts.join('')` → `parts.join('-')` | `multiples of both`, `range produces...` | ✅ |
| `String(n)` → `n` | `plain numbers come back as strings`, `range...` | ✅ |
| swap the two `if`s | `multiples of both are FizzBuzz` | ✅ |
| `n % 3` → `n % 4` | three tests | ✅ |
| `parts.length > 0` → `parts.length >= 0` | all plain-number tests | ✅ |
| `n <= end` → `n < end` in the range | `range produces one entry per number` | ✅ |
| `let n = start` → `let n = start + 1` | `range produces one entry per number` | ✅ |

**WHY:** this is the real measure of a test suite. Not "how many tests are there" — a hundred tests that all check the same line are one test. The question is: **what could I break without anything going red?** Every uncaught mutation is a hole where a future bug can walk in unnoticed.

The five shipped tests catch all eight mutations, which is a genuinely good result for a suite this size, and it's not an accident — they were chosen to cover distinct *categories* (plain, Fizz, Buzz, both, range) rather than accumulated by adding whatever came to mind.

**Try to find a mutation that survives.** There are some. Changing `100` to `99` in `cli.js` breaks nothing, because `cli.js` has no tests — which is precisely the gap exercise 9 fills. Making `fizzbuzz` return `'FIZZ'` for `n === 1000000` also survives, since nothing tests values that large. Whether either matters is a judgement call, and making that call consciously is the skill.

Real mutation-testing tools (Stryker for JavaScript) automate this: they generate hundreds of mutations, run your suite against each, and report a "mutation score." Doing it by hand a few times teaches you what the number means, which is worth more than the number.

### 13. Rules as inspectable data

```js
export const CLASSIC_RULES = [[3, 'Fizz'], [5, 'Buzz']];

export function describeRules(rules) {
  const lines = rules.map(([d, w]) => `Multiples of ${d} → ${w}`);
  lines.push('Everything else → the number itself');
  return lines.join('\n');
}
```

```js
test('describes the classic rules', () => {
  assert.equal(
    describeRules(CLASSIC_RULES),
    'Multiples of 3 → Fizz\nMultiples of 5 → Buzz\nEverything else → the number itself'
  );
});

test('an empty rule set is just the fallback', () => {
  assert.equal(describeRules([]), 'Everything else → the number itself');
});
```

**WHY:** this function is *impossible* to write against `original.js`. The rules there exist only as control flow — as the shape of an `if`/`else` tree — and control flow can be executed but not read. You cannot ask an `if` statement what it checks.

Once the rules are an array, they're an ordinary value, and everything you can do to a value becomes available: print it (this exercise), validate it (reject a divisor of 0 before it causes a division problem), serialise it to JSON and load it from a config file, let a user edit it in a form, diff two versions to see what changed between releases, or generate documentation from it automatically.

That progression — **behaviour → data → everything data can do** — is one of the highest-leverage moves in programming, and you'll meet it repeatedly in this repo:

- `10-rpn-calculator` dispatches operators from a table, so adding one is a row.
- `13-cipher-suite` gives every cipher the same shape so they're interchangeable values.
- `40-state-machine` encodes transitions as data, which makes the machine *drawable*.
- `31-validator` builds validation rules as composable data.
- `typescript/32-typed-actions` puts a type system on top of exactly this idea.

**The counter-pressure, so you don't overdo it.** Data-driven code is harder to read than a straightforward `if` when there are only two cases, and stack traces through a generic dispatcher are worse than stack traces through named functions. Reach for it when the rule set genuinely varies, when someone outside the code needs to see or edit it, or when you're on the third near-identical branch. Not on the first. Project 04 is the whole lesson on that restraint — the rule of three.

# 01 — FizzBuzz

**Lesson: separate *computing an answer* from *printing it*, and set up a test workflow.**

New to JavaScript? Read [`LEARN.md`](LEARN.md) first — it teaches every concept this page assumes. Then come back here, then do [`PRACTICE.md`](PRACTICE.md).

## Run it

```
node 01-fizzbuzz/original.js
node 01-fizzbuzz/refactored/cli.js
node --test "01-fizzbuzz/**/*.test.js"
```

⚠️ Quote the glob. On Node 22+, `node --test 01-fizzbuzz/` resolves the folder as a module and fails. `npm test` from the repo root runs everything.

## What's wrong with the original?

Nothing is *broken* — it prints the right output. But ask: **how would you test it?**
You can't. The only way to check it is to run it and read 100 lines with your eyes.
The logic (what to say for each number) and the output (`console.log`) are welded together.

That question — *how would I test this?* — is the tool this whole repo is built around. It looks like a question about testing and it isn't; it's a question about structure. Code you can't test is code where the deciding and the doing are tangled, and tangled code is code that's expensive to change. The test is only the messenger.

Smaller issues that compound in bigger programs:

- `var` leaks out of the loop; `let` is block-scoped and what you want by default.
- `==` does type coercion (`"3" == 3` is true). Always use `===` so comparisons mean
  what they say.
- The `i % 3 == 0 && i % 5 == 0` branch **duplicates** the other two conditions. If the
  rules change ("also Bazz for 7"), you now edit an exploding number of combined branches:
  3 rules = 8 branches.

### The branch order is load-bearing

Worth pausing on, because it's the subtlest problem here. The combined `&&` branch has to come **first**. Move it below the `% 3` check and 15 prints `Fizz` — silently, with every individual line still looking correct. The bug lives in the *relationship between* the branches, not in any one of them, which makes it invisible to a line-by-line review.

Bugs that exist between lines rather than in them are the expensive kind. The refactor removes the possibility entirely.

### The combination explosion, counted

| Rules | Branches (original's style) | Lines (refactor's style) |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 4 | 2 |
| 3 | 8 | 3 |
| 4 | 16 | 4 |
| 5 | 32 | 5 |

2ⁿ against n. This is what "good design" concretely means: not elegance, but which changes are cheap. The refactor makes *adding a rule* cheap, because that's the change this program will actually be asked for.

### And it produces no data

The original computes each line and immediately throws it at the terminal. At no point does the program hold the answer. So "how many Fizzes are there?", "give me the first ten", "render this into HTML" are all unanswerable without a rewrite — not because they're hard, but because the sequence never exists as a value.

## What changed in the refactor

```
refactored/
├── fizzbuzz.js       ← the rules. Pure. Never prints.
├── cli.js            ← the printing. Two lines.
└── fizzbuzz.test.js  ← the checks.
```

1. **`fizzbuzz(n)` is a pure function** — number in, string out, no printing. Pure
   functions are trivially testable: call them, assert on the return value. That's the
   whole test file.
2. **The "build up parts" pattern kills the combination explosion.** Each rule is one
   independent `if`. Adding "Bazz for 7" is one new line, not a rewrite of the branch tree.
3. **`cli.js` is the only file that touches the console**, and it's 2 lines. When the
   I/O layer is that thin, bugs have nowhere to hide.

### The whole trick is a missing `else`

```js
const parts = [];
if (n % 3 === 0) parts.push('Fizz');   // no else
if (n % 5 === 0) parts.push('Buzz');   // no else
return parts.length > 0 ? parts.join('') : String(n);
```

Two independent `if` statements instead of a chain. For n = 15 both run, `parts` becomes `['Fizz', 'Buzz']`, and `join('')` produces `'FizzBuzz'` without anyone having written the word `FizzBuzz` anywhere.

**The combinations moved out of the code and into the data.** Code that enumerates cases grows exponentially with the number of cases; code that accumulates data grows linearly. That sentence generalizes far past FizzBuzz — any time you find yourself writing branches for combinations of conditions, this is the move.

A consequence worth naming: reordering the two `if`s now changes only the *order of the words* (`BuzzFizz` instead of `FizzBuzz`), never whether a rule applies. Order went from a correctness concern to a cosmetic one. That's one entire class of bug deleted, permanently.

### Why `String(n)` and not `n`

So the return type never varies. A function that returns a string sometimes and a number other times forces every caller to defend itself, and breaks the moment someone writes `fizzbuzz(4).toUpperCase()`. Seven characters, one class of caller bug gone. (The TypeScript track turns this discipline into a compile-time guarantee.)

### Why `fizzbuzzRange` returns an array, not a string

Because an array is the more structured thing, and the caller can always flatten it. `cli.js` joins it with newlines; a test compares it element by element; the stats exercise in PRACTICE.md counts it. Had it returned pre-joined text, every one of those would have to split it apart again.

**Return the most structured form you have; let the caller flatten it.**

### The shape

```
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  fizzbuzz.js       PURE — testable      │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    ▲               ▲
     ┌──────────────┴───┐   ┌───────┴────────────┐
     │  cli.js          │   │  fizzbuzz.test.js  │
     │  IMPURE — prints │   │  the safety net    │
     └──────────────────┘   └────────────────────┘
```

The core doesn't know it's being printed and doesn't know it's being tested. Both are just clients of the same interface — which is exactly why adding a third (an HTTP endpoint, a web page, another program) costs nothing.

## Designs deliberately not taken

- **`if (n % 15 === 0)`** — shorter and readable, but it's the combination explosion in disguise. Add a third rule and you're writing checks for 105, 21, and 35. The `15` also quietly assumes 3 and 5 are coprime, which isn't true for every pair of rules you might add.
- **A string accumulator** (`let out = ''; out += 'Fizz'`) — genuinely fine, same design. The array keeps the pieces separate one moment longer, which matters the instant someone wants `'Fizz-Buzz'` or the pieces as a list.
- **A rules lookup table** — arguably the best design, and where PRACTICE.md exercise 4 leads. Not shipped here because it needs `filter`, `map`, and destructuring in project 01. Project 10 introduces it properly.
- **A function that prints** — the most common half-refactor. It looks like progress because there's a function now, but there's still no return value to check. Extracting code only helps if you also extract the *decision*.

## Where this pattern goes

The same split, at full scale:

| Real system | Pure core | Impure shell |
|---|---|---|
| Web server (`65-rest-api`) | params → result object | HTTP request/response |
| React app (`react/13-usereducer-todo`) | `(state, action) => state` | rendering to the DOM |
| Game loop (`17-snake`) | `step(state) => state` | keyboard, canvas |
| Parser (`69-json-parser`) | text → structured data | reading the file |
| Billing (`32-money-cart`) | the pricing rules | database, invoice PDF |

In every case the design was driven by the same question, and the answer was the same move.

**When it doesn't apply:** for a genuine fourteen-line throwaway you'll run once and delete, three files and a test suite is worse than one file. Ceremony costs something. The judgement is "will this be read or changed again?" — and in professional work it almost always will be, by someone who isn't you, sooner than you expect. Project 04 teaches the opposite restraint, so you get both halves.

## Key takeaway

The question "how would I test this?" is a design tool. If the answer is "I can't",
the computing and the doing are tangled, and the fix is to pull the decision-making
into a pure function. Every other project in this repo builds on that move.
